name: The Marrow Share — Collective Grief Neural Broadcast
creator: Developed by grief counselor and BCI specialist Amara Osei-Volkov following the Okonkwo-Paz Night disaster
description: In the weeks following the Lakefire Collapse of 2211, Amara Osei-Volkov designed an open neural-feed protocol allowing participants to join a shared grief state — not simulated, but a genuine pooled emotional signal composed of thousands of simultaneous BCI feeds, each contributing their actual grief in real time. The result was described as being 'held by the weight of everyone's loss at once,' and the protocol was used collectively every anniversary of the collapse for three years before spreading to other commemorative contexts. Participants could contribute as little or as much emotional signal as they chose.
medium: BCI, neural feed, collective emotional broadcast
cultural_impact: The Marrow Share established a new vocabulary for collective public mourning in a city where most grief was privatized or medicated, and generated serious ethical and clinical debate about the nature of shared affect — whether pooled grief was therapeutic, exploitative, or something for which existing frameworks were simply inadequate.
controversy: Corporate wellness platforms attempted to license the protocol for use in employee 'resilience programming,' which Osei-Volkov publicly refused; the platforms developed proprietary imitations that critics argued extracted emotional labor without consent. A small number of participants reported becoming unable to access their grief privately afterward, as if it now only existed in the shared space.
story_hooks: Amara Osei-Volkov has disappeared, and the protocol has been modified by someone unknown — the shared grief state now contains a signal that doesn't match any registered participant.
A character who contributed to the first Marrow Share finds that the grief they shared was recorded and is now being used as evidence in a corporate liability case.
Someone is using a corrupted version of the protocol not for grief but for something else — the pooled emotional signal it generates has an application Osei-Volkov never intended.
